description:
The golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos) is the most powerful raptor in Europe. A high-altitude hunter, it stoops on its prey at speeds exceeding 150 km/h, the talons exerting sufficient pressure to kill on impact.

The eagle has landed on its kill — a hare — and spreads its wings above it in the gesture of 'mantling', that instinctive movement that screens the prey from potential thieves. This is a precise and rarely depicted behaviour, that speaks of intelligence as much as of power. The diagonal composition — wing deployed from the upper right corner down to the prey at lower left — gives the full wingspan without losing the tension of the moment.

description:
The black rhinoceros (Diceros bicornis) is a critically endangered species. Smaller and more nervous than the white rhinoceros, it is known for its tendency to charge. Its two keratin horns — the main one capable of exceeding fifty centimetres — have led to it being decimated by poaching.

The animal is in movement, one foreleg raised — neither truly in charge, nor truly at rest. That ambiguity is what was sought: a rhinoceros in action, but the action suspended. The pencil work bears down on the mass of the body, the thick skin rendered by interlocking hatching, while the legs and vegetation remain as sketches, to concentrate all the weight on the volume of the body.

description:
The African buffalo (Syncerus caffer) is one of the most dangerous animals in Africa. Old solitary males, nicknamed 'dagga boys', are particularly unpredictable. The 'boss' — the broad horn-base that fuses together at the top of the skull — is the mark of the adult and one of the most recognisable animal forms on the continent.

It is coming straight towards us. No flight, no hesitation — only this frontal mass, the boss dominating the head, the eyes sunk beneath the horns. The frontal choice is deliberate: it is the only angle that gives the full amplitude of the horns and the full threat of the silhouette. The drawing does not seek the beauty of the buffalo — it seeks its weight.

description:
The red deer (Cervus elaphus) is the largest deer in Europe. In September and October, the male enters the rut and 'bells' — a bellow that carries for several kilometres, a signal of attraction for the hinds and of warning for rivals.

The head thrown back, the throat open, the tines raised above: this is the bellow at its moment of greatest charge in the deer's whole life. The jaw wide open, the eye turned upward — everything speaks the physiological tension of this call. The pencil concentrates its work on the head and chest, letting the background dissolve, so that nothing distracts attention from this moment of raw power.

description:
The title owes nothing to chance. During the rut, from mid-September to early October, the male deer abandons all discretion. It bellows, it charges, it defends its territory — and mates with as many does as possible. Faithless by nature, by necessity, by instinct. The name says something true about this animal that the hunting tradition has always clothed in a form of virile grandeur.

This painting has a particular history: it was made as part of a fifty-two-minute documentary for the Seasons channel, directed by David Flacard and Laurent Buchemeyer. For six months, they followed me — from the first observations of the rut in the northern Médoc through to the presentation of the finished painting at the Game Fair in Lamotte Beuvron. A long, immersive process that always begins by listening before painting.

For the composition, I chose maximum close-up. The deer does not fit within the frame — it overflows it. The head raised, the mouth wide open in the cry of the rut, the antlers spreading across the full width of the horizontal format: everything is excess, disproportion, urgency. This is the instant when the animal is most itself — and least discreet.

The light of the damp Médoc morning is what I sought to render above all. Not a clear light — a diffuse, blue-toned light that envelops the deer in mist and makes its breath appear like a flame. The palette is deliberately restrained: grey, beige, warm ochre on the antlers. Oil paint allows one to work these subtle gradations, these imperceptible passages between fur and fog, between the animal and its environment.

description:
'Dust Rage' is a contraction. Dust — the cloud of dust that a charging rhinoceros raises like a war cloud. And Rage — my anger at poaching, that industrial slaughter that massacres rhinoceroses for their horn, a simple mass of keratin sold at exorbitant prices with no scientific justification whatsoever. This title is as much a state of mind as a painting title.

But this painting is above all a defiant gesture against those who would reduce this animal to a trophy or a commodity. This rhinoceros is alive, sovereign, magnificent. It is in the foreground, it occupies all the space, it charges. That charge is not a threat — it is an answer. An answer of irrefutable beauty to the ugliness of those who hunt it.

I chose the face-to-face with no stepping back. The rhinoceros overflows the frame — it takes up space, it invades. The dust envelops the scene in an atmosphere of total movement, almost audible. The brutal foreground, the mass of the body, the gaze — everything gives that feeling of absolute presence, impossible to avoid.

The light is dry, direct, African. It cuts the volumes of the skin with precision — every fold, every crack of the hide. But hyperrealism is not an end in itself: it serves emotion. To render this rhinoceros so concrete and tangible is to refuse to let it become abstract — to reduce it to a number in a poaching report.

description:
There is something particular about the old solitary boar. Driven from the groups, retreated into the densest parts of the forest, it has developed an intelligence and a wariness that the young do not yet have. Hunters call it 'la bête noire'. The title imposed itself as I painted: Bad Lieutenant — not the corrupt cop, but the lone cop who acts by his own rules and dispenses his own justice.

The scene takes place in winter, in a forest that does not belong to everyone. The snow is deep, but the boar advances — head high, proud, with that muted and inexorable energy that characterises the animal. An advance that nothing seems able to stop.

The panoramic format embraces the horizontal movement of the animal. The contrast is radical: the dark, massive body against the whiteness of the snow, the forest dissolving into darkness behind it. The snow thrown up by its own paws creates an atmosphere of raw power. I worked the texture of the coat with care — those stiff, dense, almost mineral bristles that make the wild boar so particular.

This painting is an ode to the wild animal in its most radical element: winter, forest, snow. No golden light, no shimmering colours. Just black, white, and that energy that nothing seems able to stop. Bad Lieutenant does not pose for the painting. It passes through.

description:
The Zambezi is one of those rivers that structures southern Africa as much as it traverses it. Elephants cross it regularly, often in groups, in a relative silence that contrasts with the power of what one observes. Three of them, here. Water at mid-body, tusks catching the light, trunks raised.

What stopped me in this scene is the way the bodies organise themselves naturally in space — almost like a considered composition, even though it is not at all. Three immense masses advancing in the same direction, and yet each with its own presence, its own relationship to the light.

The composition is resolutely horizontal, but the trunks and tusks introduce diagonals, breaks, an almost abstract graphic dynamism. I worked a great deal on texture — the thick, rough skin of the elephants, the water catching the light differently on different surfaces, the contrast between deep shadow areas and the almost white reflections on the tusks.

This painting is as much an exercise in light as a portrait of animals. At a certain level of detail, the skin of a wet elephant becomes almost an abstraction — a geography of textures and tones. That is what I wanted to explore here, and what I hope the viewer feels when they draw closer.

description:
South Africa, the Timbavati. This young male lion has been feeding on a buffalo for more than two days — there are seven of them sharing it. We observe the scene with the vultures: flies swarm, the smell is strong, almost unbearable. The lions are replete but will not leave the carcass for some time yet.

Through the buffalo's horn, the young male suddenly fixes his gaze on me. No aggression, no flight — just that calm, direct look that seems to say: 'Don't move. You're next.' It is that precise moment I wanted to paint.

The composition is built around this confrontation of gazes: the lion in the foreground, the buffalo's horn as a frame within the frame, and the eye — that yellow, fixed eye that occupies the centre of the painting. The tones are dark, warm, saturated with that afternoon African light. The texture of the coat, the blood, the dust — everything contributes to the immediacy of the scene.

I wanted the viewer to feel what I felt that day: that slight unease mingled with fascination, that privilege of being there, so close, and that absolute certainty of being at the bottom of the food chain.

description:
The buffalo does not have the look of a bovine. Every one I have ever observed had its own character, its own features, its own personality — some are handsome, others less so. But what unites them is that intensity in the eyes, a gaze that sizes you up and judges you from on high, almost human in its hardness. When Robert Ruark wrote that the buffalo 'looks at you as if you owe him money', he found the exact words for what anyone feels who has encountered that gaze.

'Last Warning' — the final warning. This big male is fixing you, evaluating you. Charge or not? Perhaps. Perhaps not. It is precisely this uncertainty that makes the animal so fascinating and so feared. I wanted to paint a buffalo with a real personality — a face whose intensity pierces through, not a generic animal. To illustrate Ruark's phrase through a painting, to render that feeling one has when a buffalo judges you with its eyes.

The panoramic format imposed itself naturally: the horns had to occupy all the space, to overflow the frame almost. The palette is cool — blues, greys, broken whites — to render the particular light of the savanna in broad daylight, and to concentrate all the tension of the painting in the single gaze of the animal. In the background, a second buffalo barely sketched in recalls that this male is not alone.

The gaze is always the starting point of my paintings. It is what hooks, questions, creates the bond between the animal and the one who looks. With Last Warning, I wanted that bond to be uncomfortable — for the viewer to feel, even for a moment, what a man feels facing a buffalo that has made up its mind.

description:
The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) uses termite mounds as natural lookout posts. Without retractile claws, it can neither defend a kill against lions nor climb trees like the leopard — its survival rests on vision and speed.

description:
Nine months without painting. Nine months setting aside the brushes, the canvases, the smell of oils. This was not a pause chosen from fatigue, but a necessity — time to understand why I paint, and where I want to go. Sunset Guardian was born of that silence. The first painting after the long parenthesis.

I wanted this lion to embody exactly what I had found during those nine months: a settled presence, without agitation. It does not look — it simply is. Seated in the evening light, it has nothing to prove. That sovereign serenity is what I was seeking to find again in myself.

The raking light of the setting sun sculpts the coat in warm touches — golds, burnt oranges, long shadows. The background dissolves into a golden haze that isolates the figure and concentrates all attention on the face. The handling is freer than my previous works, more liberated in the detail, without sacrificing the overall realism.

This painting marks a turning point in my work. After the pause, I was no longer trying to prove technique — I wanted every brushstroke to carry something true. Sunset Guardian is the first work in which I felt I had painted exactly what I felt, and not simply what I saw.

There is, in an artist's life, one work that occupies a place apart — just one, that carries all the rest. The Big One is mine. I had been thinking about this challenge for a long time. When I finally decided to take it on, I had not yet fully measured what it would represent.

One year of work. Moments of deep doubt, moments of pure joy. Dozens of tubes emptied, brushes worn to nothing — and for the upper sections, scaffolding, because the canvas is two and a half metres tall. And then that day, the final touch, which will remain etched in me as one of the most intense moments of my life as an artist. The painting now hangs in the home of a dear friend. From time to time I go to visit it. And strangely, I never tire of it.

The composition is frontal, almost symmetrical — the elephant comes straight at you, head high, ears spread, trunk low. It occupies the entire canvas, from the left edge to the right. The palette is that of the savanna in the dry season: golden ochres, warm and amber browns, a background of dry grasses that envelops the silhouette. Warm, almost luminous — and yet overwhelming.

At this scale, the painting ceases to be an object one looks at and becomes something one feels. I wanted the viewer to experience physically the presence of the animal — not to observe it from a distance, but to find oneself face to face with it, as in the bush.

description:
'Twiga' — that is the Swahili word for 'giraffe'. A word that sounds like the animal itself: tall, slender, a little off-balance in its beauty. This painting is part of the 'African Sepias' series, in which I worked with a restrained, almost monochrome palette, to get to the essence of form.

The model was six months old at the time of painting. Six months, and already three metres tall. There is something endearing in the youth of the giraffe — those still-clumsy long legs, that neck not yet fully mastered, that openness of curiosity towards the world. I wanted to fix that precise instant when the awkwardness is still visible, before definitive grace settles in.

For the composition, I chose the close portrait. The young giraffe occupies almost the entire vertical field. No landscape, no context: just it. That tightening forces the eye to settle on the details — the patches, the texture of the coat, and above all the eye, that immense and gentle eye which is perhaps the most beautiful thing about the giraffe.

The light is soft, muted, of that particular quality one finds in the late afternoon over the savannas. The sepia tones amplify this effect — they warm the scene, give it a temporal density, as if this moment already belonged to a precious past. That is what I love about this series: colour fades so that form remains.

description:
'Pembe' means 'Horn' in Swahili. One word to designate what makes the rhinoceros: what distinguishes it, what protects it, and what, today, puts it in danger.

This painting belongs to the 'African Sepias' collection — a series in which I chose to work in warm, almost monochrome harmonies, to concentrate attention on form rather than colour.

What fascinated me here is the skin. That natural armour, folded, cracked, almost mineral. I worked the raking light that highlights every relief, every fold, every fissure — as if the material itself told an entire life.

The result is less a portrait than a study of texture. The rhinoceros becomes almost abstract — a surface of stone and hide, traversed by light.

description:
'Udongo' is my first oil painting. Painting the elephant — that monumental animal, with skin thick as earth itself — imposed itself as an obvious choice to inaugurate this technique. Oil paint offers a material, a depth that acrylic cannot render in the same way. And the elephant, perhaps more than any other animal, deserved that richness.

The elephant of Udongo is not shown in motion, nor in action. It is simply there — present, massive, imperturbable. The tight framing on its skin makes the horizon, the context, the setting disappear. Nothing remains but it: that living architecture, that animated earth. 'Udongo' — earth in Swahili. It was the only possible title.

Two colours only: burnt umber and titanium white. That palette reduced to essentials is not a constraint — it is a choice. It forces you to say everything through light, contrast, and matter. The skin of the elephant, with its cracks and deep furrows, becomes a territory in itself. Through sobriety, the painting tips towards something else: you no longer know if you are looking at an animal or a mineral landscape.

With Udongo, I wanted to explore how far a stripped-down palette could go. Oil paint allowed me to work the texture in successive layers — to accumulate matter as the elephant accumulates years. This painting is a statement of intent for the entire African Sepias collection: wildlife as a pretext to explore painting in its most raw dimension.
